title: Gaps and islands: busy-day streaks

WITH d AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT ManufactureDate FROM pharma.Batches
), g AS (
    SELECT ManufactureDate,
           DATEADD(day, -ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ManufactureDate), ManufactureDate) AS grp
    FROM d
)

       MAX(ManufactureDate) AS StreakEnd,
       COUNT(*)           AS Days
FROM g
GROUP BY grp

), c AS (

title: Repeat batches within N days
q: Find batches that happened within @Days days of the same supplier's previous batch. Use @Days = 145. Show supplier, previous date, current date and gap.
sql:
DECLARE @Days int = 145;

WITH v AS (
    SELECT SupplierID, BatchID, ManufactureDate,
           LAG(ManufactureDate) OVER (PARTITION BY SupplierID ORDER BY ManufactureDate, BatchID) AS PrevDate
    FROM pharma.Batches
)
SELECT SupplierID, PrevDate, ManufactureDate,
       DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, ManufactureDate) AS GapDays
FROM v
WHERE PrevDate IS NOT NULL
  AND DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, ManufactureDate) <= @Days
ORDER BY SupplierID, ManufactureDate;
how: LAG finds the previous batch and DATEDIFF measures the gap. A variable makes the window easy to change. Repeat-activity checks like this are a common interview question.

       SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'C'  THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS CK,

  AND SCHEMA_NAME(schema_id) = 'pharma'

title: Batch chain for one supplier
q: Starting from supplier 1's first batch, use a recursive CTE to walk forward through that supplier's batches in date order, with a step number.
sql:
WITH Ordered AS (
    SELECT BatchID, ManufactureDate,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ManufactureDate, BatchID) AS rn
    FROM pharma.Batches
    WHERE SupplierID = 1
), Chain AS (
    SELECT BatchID, ManufactureDate, rn, 0 AS Step
    FROM Ordered
    WHERE rn = 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.BatchID, o.ManufactureDate, o.rn, c.Step + 1
    FROM Ordered AS o
    JOIN Chain AS c ON o.rn = c.rn + 1
)
SELECT BatchID, ManufactureDate, Step
FROM Chain
ORDER BY Step;
how: The anchor picks the starting row. The recursive part finds the next row (rn + 1) one step at a time. The same shape walks hierarchies such as org charts or bills of materials.

title: MAXRECURSION
q: Generate numbers 1 to 200 with a recursive CTE. (The default limit is 100 levels.)
sql:
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM N WHERE n < 200
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS HowMany, MAX(n) AS LastNumber
FROM N
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 200);
how: SQL Server stops recursion after 100 levels by default. OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) raises the limit; 0 means no limit, which is risky.

title: Month-over-month with a calendar
q: For all 12 months of 2024 (even empty ones), show total batch cost, previous month's total and growth %.
sql:
WITH Months AS (
    SELECT CAST('2024-01-01' AS date) AS m
    UNION ALL
    SELECT DATEADD(month, 1, m) FROM Months WHERE m < '2024-12-01'
), Totals AS (
    SELECT mo.m, ISNULL(SUM(e.BatchCost), 0) AS Total
    FROM Months AS mo
    LEFT JOIN pharma.Batches AS e
           ON e.ManufactureDate >= mo.m AND e.ManufactureDate < DATEADD(month, 1, mo.m)
    GROUP BY mo.m
)
SELECT m AS MonthStart, Total,
       LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m) AS PrevTotal,
       CAST(100.0 * (Total - LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m))
            / NULLIF(LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m), 0) AS decimal(6,1)) AS GrowthPct
FROM Totals
ORDER BY m;

title: Org-chart style hierarchy with path
q: Build a small hierarchy in a table variable (region head > team > supplier) and list it with a recursive CTE, showing each level and a path like Head > North > Olivia.
sql:
DECLARE @Org TABLE (NodeID int, ParentID int NULL, NodeName nvarchar(100));
INSERT INTO @Org VALUES (0, NULL, N'Head');
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Region), 0, Region
FROM pharma.Suppliers
GROUP BY Region;
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT 100 + p.SupplierID, r.NodeID, p.SupplierName
FROM pharma.Suppliers AS p
JOIN @Org AS r ON r.NodeName = p.Region
WHERE p.SupplierID <= 6;

WITH Tree AS (
    SELECT NodeID, NodeName, 0 AS Lvl, CAST(NodeName AS nvarchar(400)) AS PathText
    FROM @Org
    WHERE ParentID IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.NodeID, o.NodeName, t.Lvl + 1,
           CAST(t.PathText + N' > ' + o.NodeName AS nvarchar(400))
    FROM @Org AS o
    JOIN Tree AS t ON o.ParentID = t.NodeID
)
SELECT NodeID, Lvl, PathText
FROM Tree
ORDER BY PathText;

title: Script a table structure
q: Show the column list of Batches as one CREATE TABLE-style text, built from metadata.
sql:
SELECT 'CREATE TABLE pharma.Batches (' +
       STRING_AGG(CAST(c.name + ' ' + ty.name +
                  CASE WHEN ty.name IN ('varchar','nvarchar')
                       THEN '(' + CAST(CASE WHEN ty.name = 'nvarchar' THEN c.max_length / 2 ELSE c.max_length END AS varchar(5)) + ')'
                       WHEN ty.name = 'decimal' THEN '(' + CAST(c.precision AS varchar(3)) + ',' + CAST(c.scale AS varchar(3)) + ')'
                       ELSE '' END +
                  CASE WHEN c.is_nullable = 1 THEN ' NULL' ELSE ' NOT NULL' END AS varchar(max)), ', ')
       WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY c.column_id) + ');' AS Script
FROM sys.columns AS c
JOIN sys.types AS ty ON ty.user_type_id = c.user_type_id
WHERE c.object_id = OBJECT_ID('pharma.Batches');

title: MERGE: sync a staging table
q: Sync supplier regions from a staging list: update regions that changed, insert new suppliers, and report each action.
sql:
DECLARE @Stage TABLE (SupplierID int, SupplierName nvarchar(80), SupplierCode varchar(20), Region varchar(10));
INSERT INTO @Stage
SELECT SupplierID, SupplierName, SupplierCode, CASE WHEN Region = 'East' THEN 'West' ELSE 'East' END
FROM pharma.Suppliers WHERE SupplierID = 1          -- region change
UNION ALL
SELECT SupplierID, SupplierName, SupplierCode, Region
FROM pharma.Suppliers WHERE SupplierID = 2          -- no change
UNION ALL
SELECT 301, N'New Supplier', 'PS-0301', 'North';     -- new

MERGE pharma.Suppliers AS t
USING @Stage AS s
   ON t.SupplierID = s.SupplierID
WHEN MATCHED AND t.Region <> s.Region THEN
    UPDATE SET t.Region = s.Region
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (SupplierID, SupplierName, SupplierCode, Region)
    VALUES (s.SupplierID, s.SupplierName, s.SupplierCode, s.Region)
OUTPUT $action AS ActionTaken, inserted.SupplierID, deleted.Region AS OldRegion, inserted.Region AS NewRegion;
how: MERGE does insert, update and (optionally) delete in one statement. The extra `AND t.Region <> s.Region` skips rows that did not change. $action in OUTPUT reports what happened to each row.

title: Isolation levels
q: Name SQL Server's transaction isolation levels and the problem each one prevents. Show the current level.
sql:
SELECT CASE transaction_isolation_level
         WHEN 1 THEN 'READ UNCOMMITTED' WHEN 2 THEN 'READ COMMITTED'
         WHEN 3 THEN 'REPEATABLE READ'  WHEN 4 THEN 'SERIALIZABLE'
         WHEN 5 THEN 'SNAPSHOT' END AS IsolationLevel
FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions
WHERE session_id = @@SPID;
how: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads. READ COMMITTED (the default) prevents dirty reads. REPEATABLE READ also prevents non-repeatable reads. SERIALIZABLE also prevents phantom rows. SNAPSHOT reads a consistent version without blocking writers. Higher isolation means fewer anomalies but more blocking.

title: Top-earning product per region

title: Joins that multiply rows
q: Show each supplier's total batch batch cost and total number of inventory records. Make sure the batch cost is not double counted.
sql:
SELECT p.SupplierID, p.SupplierName,
       ISNULL(ch.TotalBatchCost, 0) AS TotalBatchCost,
       ISNULL(li.Inventory, 0) AS Inventory
FROM pharma.Suppliers AS p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT SupplierID, SUM(BatchCost) AS TotalBatchCost
           FROM pharma.Batches
           GROUP BY SupplierID) AS ch ON ch.SupplierID = p.SupplierID
LEFT JOIN (SELECT e.SupplierID, COUNT(*) AS Inventory
           FROM pharma.Inventory AS r
           JOIN pharma.Batches AS e ON e.BatchID = r.BatchID
           GROUP BY e.SupplierID) AS li ON li.SupplierID = p.SupplierID
ORDER BY TotalBatchCost DESC;
how: If you join Batches and Inventory first and then SUM(BatchCost), a batch with 2 inventory records has its batch cost counted twice (fan-out). Aggregating each child table separately before joining fixes this. Interviewers often test whether you spot fan-out.

title: Short-circuit is not guaranteed
q: Return warehouses where the name has a space and the text before the first space is longer than 8 characters. Write it safely so CHARINDEX never gives a negative length.
sql:
SELECT WarehouseName
FROM pharma.Warehouses
WHERE CASE WHEN CHARINDEX(' ', WarehouseName) > 0
           THEN LEN(LEFT(WarehouseName, CHARINDEX(' ', WarehouseName) - 1))
           ELSE 0
      END > 8;
how: SQL Server does not promise to evaluate AND conditions left to right, so `CHARINDEX(...) > 0 AND LEN(LEFT(... - 1)) > 8` could still error on a row with no space. A CASE expression controls the order. This is a senior-level detail.

title: NOT IN and the NULL trap
q: Interview trap: show why NOT IN fails when the list contains NULL. Find batches that are not a parent of any other batch, first with NOT IN (wrong), then with NOT EXISTS (right).
sql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pharma.Batches AS e
   WHERE e.BatchID NOT IN (SELECT ParentBatchID
                               FROM pharma.Batches)) AS NotIn_Wrong,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pharma.Batches AS e
   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pharma.Batches AS c
                     WHERE c.ParentBatchID = e.BatchID)) AS NotExists_Right;
how: ParentBatchID is NULL on every row here. `x NOT IN (..., NULL)` is never true, so NOT IN returns 0. NOT EXISTS ignores the NULLs and correctly finds that no batch is a parent. You can also fix NOT IN by adding `WHERE ParentBatchID IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery.

title: IN vs EXISTS vs JOIN
q: Return suppliers with at least one Pending batch three ways (IN, EXISTS, JOIN with DISTINCT). Each should return the same count.
sql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pharma.Suppliers
   WHERE SupplierID IN (SELECT SupplierID FROM pharma.Batches
                       WHERE Status = 'Pending')) AS ViaIn,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pharma.Suppliers AS p
   WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pharma.Batches AS e
                 WHERE e.SupplierID = p.SupplierID AND e.Status = 'Pending')) AS ViaExists,
  (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT p.SupplierID)
   FROM pharma.Suppliers AS p
   JOIN pharma.Batches AS e ON e.SupplierID = p.SupplierID
   WHERE e.Status = 'Pending') AS ViaJoin;
how: All three give the same answer. A plain JOIN repeats a supplier for each matching batch, which is why DISTINCT is needed. IN and EXISTS never duplicate rows.

title: Above their group's average
q: List batches whose batch cost is more than the average batch cost of their own batch type.
sql:
SELECT e.BatchID, e.BatchType, e.BatchCost
FROM pharma.Batches AS e
WHERE e.BatchCost > (SELECT AVG(x.BatchCost) FROM pharma.Batches AS x
                  WHERE x.BatchType = e.BatchType)
ORDER BY e.BatchType, e.BatchCost DESC, e.BatchID;
how: The correlated subquery calculates the average for the current row's type. AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) is the window-function alternative.
